title: Global fit: χ², RMSEA, CFI, TLI and SRMR
summary: Fit indices summarise how far the model-implied covariances are from the observed ones; their cut-offs are context-dependent heuristics, not tests of truth.

body.text: The [[chi-square-test]] tests whether the model reproduces the population covariances exactly; with large samples it rejects even trivial misfit. Approximate indices complement it: [[rmsea]] measures misfit per degree of freedom (Steiger 1990; Browne & Cudeck 1993), [[cfi]] and [[tli]] compare the model with a baseline model of uncorrelated indicators (Bentler 1990), and [[srmr]] is the root mean square of the differences between observed and implied correlations.

body.explanation: χ² is the model test statistic, df its degrees of freedom and N the sample size (SEM Lab follows lavaan in using N). Values near 0 mean little misfit per degree of freedom.

body.caption: Starts at the two-factor CFA (RMSEA ≈ .013, CFI ≈ .999). Increase χ² to see how both indices respond.

body.text: Hu and Bentler (1999) proposed combinations such as CFI ≥ .95, RMSEA ≤ .06 and SRMR ≤ .08 for ML with continuous data. These came from specific simulation conditions; misfit detection depends on sample size, degrees of freedom and loading size, so the values are heuristics, not golden rules (Marsh et al. 2004). Good fit does not prove a model: equivalent models fit identically, and fit says nothing about R².

mistake.title: Using fit indices as pass/fail stamps
mistake.text: A CFI of .951 is not "valid" and .949 "invalid". Report several indices with the χ² test, examine where the misfit lies (residuals), and remember that a well-fitting model can still be wrong.

tryIt.task: Run CB-SEM on the two-factor model and read χ², df, RMSEA, CFI, TLI and SRMR. Then build a one-factor model with all eight items (next lesson's starter does this for you) and compare.

checks.question: χ² = 50, df = 20, N = 200. What is the RMSEA (lavaan convention with N)?

options.feedback: Check the numerator: it is χ² − df = 30, not χ² / df.
Remember to divide by df · N before taking the square root.

checks.question: Which statement about the Hu and Bentler (1999) cut-offs is correct?

options.text: They are heuristics derived from particular simulation conditions and should not be applied mechanically.
A model meeting all of them is the correct model.
options.feedback: Fit cannot rule out equivalent or alternative models.

options.text: They apply equally to PLS-SEM results.
options.feedback: They were developed for ML CB-SEM; PLS fit measures have different properties.
